extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, corporate communicators, crisis managers and digital strategists
extracted.subtask_description: A case-study style analysis of a corporate PR crisis (United Airlines Flight 3411) with prescriptive crisis-communication guidelines for companies and communicators. Focuses on initial response, social media dynamics, internal messaging, and broader reputational effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate unreserved apology that acknowledges harm
rubrics_metrics.description: The first official response should have offered an unreserved apology to Dr Dao and his wife after he was forcibly removed from his seat and dragged down the aircraft aisle. Instead Oscar Munoz failed to acknowledge the injuries Dr Dao suffered, apologising only for having to 're-accommodate customers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First public statement should directly apologise to affected individuals and acknowledge any injuries or harm; avoid euphemistic or transactional language (e.g. 're-accommodate customers'). A delayed or partial apology risks amplifying backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond quickly to incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: United Airlines should have moved much more quickly to limit damage from the video. This fiasco demonstrates the importance of a company's first response and how it is delivered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act fast to contain narratives before they trend: issue a timely statement, reach out directly to impacted people, and set out immediate next steps. Speed reduces the window in which damaging social-media narratives form and spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications must show empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies' response must show empathy. The lack of empathy in United Airlines response added fuel to the fire and caused another wave of backlash towards the company on social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human-centered language that recognises victims' experiences; avoid defensive or minimizing phrasing. Empathy in tone can reduce outrage even when facts are still being established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the facts straight before communicating
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the facts straight so that as a company you are fully aware of every detail of the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify what happened internally (medical status, sequence of events, policies invoked) before making definitive public statements. Accurate initial facts reduce the chance of later contradictions and further loss of trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent with the media
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, open information about the incident and the company's actions. Transparency helps control the narrative and demonstrates accountability; opacity invites speculation and fuels negative coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Own mistakes, apologise, and implement corrective procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Own your response. If the company made a mistake, own it, apologise for it and put in place the necessary procedures so it does not happen again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly accept responsibility when appropriate, outline concrete remedial actions, and communicate follow-up steps to prevent recurrence. Promises to 'do better' should be accompanied by measurable actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume incidents can go viral — recognise social media power and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: This incident highlights the power of social media, and how one isolated incident can become a global PR disaster overnight. Not only was it seen by so many, once the videos are on social media they are permanently memorialised on there, and United Airlines has no control or ability to take them down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for instantaneous, widespread dissemination (smartphones, multiple witnesses). Prepare rapid-response social-media strategies and accept that content will persist; focus on narrative management rather than attempting removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid defensive internal messaging and victim-blaming (and control leaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: An internal email from Munoz to United Airlines staff which was leaked described the passenger as 'disruptive and belligerent.' This lack of empathy in United Airlines response added fuel to the fire and caused another wave of backlash towards the company on social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure internal communications use measured, non-blaming language and anticipate leaks; inconsistent internal vs external messages damage credibility. Train staff and leadership on empathetic internal phrasing during incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about policies and selection procedures that may be scrutinised
rubrics_metrics.description: Customers have long known about the practice of 'bumping'... but never before have the exact details of how passengers are chosen to be bumped and the procedure of offering different amounts of incentives been such public knowledge. After this incident customers will now know if they wait longer the airline will offer more money to bump them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively explain operational policies that could be exposed in an incident (e.g., overbooking/bumping procedures, compensation rules). Transparency about decision criteria and fair compensation can reduce surprise and backlash; consider policy change where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider international and market-specific reputational impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The video of the incident attracted huge attention in China, which is a key growth market for United Airlines. Dr Dao’s claim that he was targeted for removal because he is Asian will likely adversely affect United’s business in Asia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how incidents will be perceived across different markets and cultural contexts. Tailor messaging and outreach to sensitive regions and be prepared for amplified effects in key markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain heightened vigilance when the company is in the spotlight — secondary incidents are magnified
rubrics_metrics.description: One month after the incident a giant rabbit died on United Airlines flight from London to Chicago. An incident like this would not normally make international news but while the world is watching every move United Airlines makes any incident or mistake is shown to the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that once brand trust is damaged, even unrelated mishaps will be magnified. Increase quality control, customer-care monitoring, and proactive communications during post-crisis periods to prevent additional reputation erosion.
